item.title: Backed by Samsung, SK Hynix, and the Korean government, Rebellions CEO Sunghyun Park wants to prove sovereign AI pays off
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of a significant business development with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Few corporate rivalries are as fierce as the one between Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The world’s leading manufacturer of memory chips and the world’s leading manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, respectively, are fighting for the title of South Korea’s most valuable company. In one area, though, the two are on the same team: Both back Rebellions, the $2.3 billion chip startup cofounded by Sunghyun Park—a veteran of Intel, SpaceX, and Morgan Stanley—that fronts South Korea’s push for sovereign silicon or AI chips that don’t depend on market leader Nvidia or any other U.S. or Chinese company.

Park’s company sits at the center of government policy. “AI requires huge capital and huge talent,” he says. “Instead of having multiple players compete, the Korean government said, ‘We need one champion. SK Hynix, please help him. Samsung, please help him. SK Telecom, KT’—top two data center companies—‘please become Rebellions’ customers.’”

Rebellions may be the clearest test of whether sovereign AI can produce something more than an expensive also-ran. Korea is funneling its best resources toward Rebellions: Samsung’s foundries, SK Hynix’s memory, and government money. The Korea National Growth Fund co-led Rebellions’ $400 million round in March.

Will it pay off? Rebellions eventually wants public investors to back a risky bet on a chip startup in a market that—for now—is skeptical of AI stocks. Still, Park is hopeful. Rebellions’ backers make it “more powerful compared to any other player in the United States,” he says. But market volatility and a wave of shelved data center IPOs will put his confidence to the test.

Park took the long road to national-champion-in-waiting. A graduate of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, he spent his compulsory military service in Afghanistan alongside the U.S. Army, where he learned English. Afterward, he earned a PhD in electrical engineering and computer science at MIT, and worked in chip engineering roles at Intel, SpaceX, and Morgan Stanley in the U.S. before returning to Korea to launch Rebellions.

Park and his cofounders—including Jinwook Oh, who designed AI chips at IBM, and Hyo-eun Kim, who developed deep-learning technology at a medical AI startup—founded Rebellions in 2020. It’s a “fabless” chip startup in that it handles only design and contracts manufacturing (or “fabrication”) out to a third party—in this case, Samsung.

In 2024, Rebellions merged with Sapeon, another chip designer backed by the SK Group. Samsung invested in the combined company in 2025.

Rebellions is part of a wave of startups challenging Nvidia by going after inference—what happens when someone uses ChatGPT, Claude, or DeepSeek—rather than training, which builds the models.

Inference is “highly cost-sensitive,” says Rakesh Kumar, a University of Illinois engineering professor and author of The Chip Age: How Semiconductors Became the World’s Most Powerful Resource. A $2 difference in price could be the reason someone chooses OpenAI over Anthropic.

Park, too, is pitching efficiency, rather than pure power. “From the hardware side, we claim only one metric,” he says. “Tokens per second, per dollar, per watt.”

Outside the U.S. and China—the clear leaders in the AI race—countries are trying to figure out how they can insulate themselves from the whims of foreign suppliers and governments.

South Korea may take the idea most seriously. It has run a state-backed Korean-language-model competition since June 2025, and its “AI for All” initiative plans to give Koreans free local chatbots. Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered AI counts only three countries with more than a handful of “notable AI models”: the U.S., with 59; China, with 35; and South Korea, with eight.

“Even my mom talks about sovereign AI, [and] she doesn’t know what sovereign AI is,” Park says.

The catch is that sovereign AI programs may lead to models and chips that are less capable, less efficient, and more costly than what comes out of the U.S. or China. Such startups can’t take advantage of the same economies of scale as established players and are selling their products to a smaller customer base. “You’re spending all this money with no guarantee of success,” Kumar says. Without Nvidia’s scale, “you might actually have higher costs.”

Rebellions, which counts backers KT and SK Telecom as customers, hopes to list in Seoul next year, though Park says it will depend on market conditions. The government wants a Korean listing first—for “national security”—before a second listing abroad, he says.

Other AI IPOs have gone astray. At least three AI-related companies—Australia’s Firmus and AirTrunk, and SK Hynix’s U.S. unit Solidigm—suspended their IPOs in October, citing market uncertainty. Investors have also punished AI shares amid worries about high debt and massive capital expenditure.

Park is unfazed by market swings—perhaps a benefit of having the Korean government and the country’s two most valuable companies as backers. But he knows that AI firms will eventually have to prove they can turn a profit. He expects the judgment to come by 2029: “Then, the market will test whether these investments are paying off or not.”

Brainstorm Tech International will convene CEOs and founders, technologists and investors, thinkers and doers to tackle the challenge of turning technological promise into lasting business and societal value. December 2 in Macau. Apply here.

item.title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant economic event with useful vocabulary and context.

Energy bills to rise by 26% from January

Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January, under regulator Ofgem's new price cap.

A typical annual bill will increase by about Â£37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although individual households costs will depend on how much they use at the coldest time of year.

Ofgem said that, for a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales paying by direct debit for gas and electricity, the increase would mean an annual bill would rise from Â£1,723 to Â£2,166 if this level was sustained for a year.

The government will make a Â£100 payment to millions of households from 4 January to help cover winter costs, in addition to an ongoing VAT cut on electricity.

Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

Ofgem said the rise had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war.

The warm home discount will also take Â£150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.

"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said: "Conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy costs higher, and we know this price increase will be a worry for many households as winter approaches.

"We urge anyone who is struggling to afford their energy bills to reach out to their supplier, who must offer appropriate support and advice. We are writing to suppliers today to remind them of their obligations and ensure they are ready to provide that support."

The increase is the largest seen since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices significantly. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest and use is peaking.

Individual usage differs, so for every Â£100 spent on energy now, the new cost will be about Â£126.

People on prepayment meters will be hit as spending comes when energy is needed, rather than spreading the cost over the year.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills.

"For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets," she said.

Andrew Bowie, shadow energy secretary, said: "It is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes onto bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher.

"Labour are utterly out of touch and could fix this tomorrow if they had the backbone."

US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners

The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.

The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.

Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.

While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.

Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, which remain locked in a trade dispute.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.

In the run up to the Shenzhen summit, the US accused China of not fully living up to the terms of what it agreed in October 2025.

Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".

However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.

The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

item.title: What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed explanation of energy cap changes with useful vocabulary and context.

What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?

Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.

The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.

It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.

What is the energy cap and how is it changing?

The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.

It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months, external.

It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.

Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.

The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about Â£45 a year from a typical bill.

Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a Â£100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.

The typical annual usage figure applies to the first category: dual-fuel households on a standard variable tariff which pay by direct debit.

But customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy used and how they pay for it.

The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs do not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.

Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.

What is a typical household?

Although the price cap sets the unit prices for gas and electricity, your household's actual bill depends on the overall amount of energy you use, and how you pay for it.

Where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.

The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.

The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.

In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.

Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.

Should I take a meter reading when the energy cap changes?

Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.

This is especially important when prices go up.

Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.

What are standing charges and how are they changing?

Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region, external and payment method.

Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers will be 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.

The electricity charge is lower than the amount charged in the previous three-month period, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.

Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.

The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen

Should I fix my energy prices?

Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period â often a year, or longer â but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.

You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind.

Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees.

What else has changed about the way energy bills are calculated?

Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills.

Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households.

However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising.

In December 2025, Ofgem approved a Â£28bn investment to improve the electricity and gas grids in Great Britain to strengthen energy supplies and protect customers against volatile energy prices. It will also reduce Britain's dependence on gas.

Customers will pay part of the cost of the upgrade, through an additional Â£108 added to energy bills by 2031.

These charges started to appear from April 2026, adding about Â£6 a month to the bill for a typical household covered by the energy cap.

What help can I get with energy bills?

Suppliers must offer customers affordable payment plans or repayment holidays if they are struggling to pay their bills. Most also offer hardship grants.

Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, and since then unpaid bills and charges have shot up.

Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, has advice for people who may be struggling:

- Take stock of all household money coming in and going out…

item.title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Personal stories on energy-saving practices with useful vocabulary and context.

'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down

Domestic energy prices are set to soar in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.

With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?

The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.

'We power down at peak times'

Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.

The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of Â£60,000.

She currently pays about Â£154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.

The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.

To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically Â£138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill.

The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.

They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.

"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.

'We've turned the heating down by 2.5C'

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay Â£1,800 for energy this year, up Â£400 on last year.

Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.

She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.

She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.

"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."

'I order heating oil in bulk'

Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.

"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.

"At the height of the Iran war it went up to Â£1.20 or Â£1.30 and now it's stabilised at around Â£1."

To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.

Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.

Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.

Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.

item.title: Why more Americans are choosing to pay over time
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of a payment trend with useful vocabulary and context.

Paying with a credit card for lunch is routine today. It wasn’t always so. In a 1993 television report covering Burger King’s trial acceptance of credit cards, one customer objected, saying, “I think it’s pretty bad if you have to use a credit card when you go to a fast food restaurant. For something as little as $3.10.” Her objection assumed using credit for a small purchase meant you could not afford it. Newer payment tools face that same assumption today, even though the ways people manage everyday spending have changed.

Today we see a major shift in how people across income levels access wages they have already earned and use deferred-payment options instead of traditional financing like credit cards. Block recently surveyed deferred-payment users, finding that 49% used cash advances or early wage access in the past year, alongside growing adoption of buy now, pay later. Survey findings also show about two in five Afterpay Pay in 4 and Pay Monthly users reported household incomes of $100,000 or more, underscoring that these tools reach across income brackets rather than serving only people without other options.

The common thread behind both habits is timing. People often have money on the way that has not hit their account yet, and they use these tools to line up an expense with an incoming paycheck. By our estimate, U.S. workers at any given time have earned about $260 billion in wages they have not yet been paid. Among surveyed deferred-payment users, 65% financed an expense at least once in the past year because money was coming from a paycheck, refund, or another source, but had not arrived yet.

That timing helps explain why many consumers are moving away from revolving card balances. Federal Reserve survey data shows the same share of credit cardholders who carried a balance at some point in the year fell from 57% to 45% over the past decade. Over a shorter span, adult use of buy now, pay later rose from 10% in 2021 to 16% in 2025, according to the Federal Reserve. When carrying a card balance is costly, a plan with a defined cost and payoff date can become more attractive.

When we ask customers what they want from a payment plan, predictability wins. In our study, 57% preferred a fixed payment schedule with the same amount, the same date and a clear endpoint over payment flexibility. One customer in our research put it plainly, saying, “We could probably buy this upfront, but then we’d be talking about a cushion of 200, 300 dollars at the end of October, which is probably cutting it too close.” Spreading payments lets households protect a cash buffer instead of draining their account at once.

In many situations, these products provide consumers a lifeline, but at other times, they simply provide choice. In the same study, 53% of respondents’ most recent financed transactions were necessity-driven, where available funds could not cover the expense when needed, while 47% were ones the customer could have paid upfront. Those numbers describe different situations, not different types of people. The same customer can use a payment plan out of necessity one month and to preserve savings the next.

Importantly, these consumers are building a habit of repayment, but traditional credit files miss so much of this picture. Legacy scoring models look backward at reported debt, treating a thin borrowing history as a lack of creditworthiness even when someone earns steady income and pays bills on time. Our underwriting models consider current cash flow, historical cash flow trends, and a customer’s debt history. By weighing the frequency and stability of incoming deposits against recurring commitments, we can spot repayment capacity a static credit report overlooks. That ongoing view also lets us reduce a limit when incoming cash slows, keeping commitments aligned with what a customer can handle.

For credit to fit how money actually moves, regulation has to keep pace with how these products work. Policymakers should support the responsible use of cash-flow data in underwriting so capable borrowers are not shut out for lacking a traditional credit file. Regulators should also judge financial products by what they actually do, including loan size, duration, cost and repayment structure, rather than forcing them into roles built for older categories. Clear disclosures should state the total dollar cost, payment due dates, when repayment ends and what happens if a payment is missed so every customer knows the full commitment before they agree.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune. This report has been updated to add more context to Block’s underwriting models and a range of considerations including current cash flow, historical cash flow trends, and a customer’s debt history.

item.title: Unpacking President Trump's financial stake in Nvidia
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of a political figure's financial stake with some useful vocabulary and context.

Unpacking President Trump's financial stake in Nvidia

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Let's connect a few things we know about this whole Nvidia situation. One is that President Trump said he convinced Nvidia's board of directors to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. Another is that Trump, or the people who manage his money, have purchased a lot of Nvidia stock since this second term began. One more thing to consider. Nvidia's stock price has roughly tripled over the past three years during the AI investment boom and as Jensen Huang has become a trusted advisor to the Trump White House. So how should we think about all this? We're going to bring in Dan Alexander, a senior editor at Forbes, who oversees coverage of money and politics. He's also an MS NOW contributor. Thanks for coming by.

DAN ALEXANDER: Sure thing. Thank you.

DETROW: Is there a number or a stat that you can cite that best represents President Trump's holdings in Nvidia?

ALEXANDER: I'm going to give you a range, unfortunately.

DETROW: OK.

ALEXANDER: But the latest reporting suggests that the range of his holdings is roughly 5 to $54 million. The stock price is moving a lot each year day.

DETROW: Sure.

ALEXANDER: So that's a number that is big, but also undetermined. And keep in mind that Trump's overall liquid holdings are roughly $2 billion.

DETROW: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: So it's a component of a much larger picture.

DETROW: So this is a large amount of money, incredible wealth for most people. But in the scheme of Donald Trump's holdings, not the biggest asset.

ALEXANDER: Not the biggest asset by a long shot. But that doesn't necessarily mean that he doesn't think about the fact that it's an asset.

DETROW: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: And particularly if it's on the higher end of that range, I mean, you know, $50 million certainly matters to Donald Trump.

DETROW: Yeah. I mean, the range that you're giving comes from financial disclosures, right?

ALEXANDER: Yes, from a combination of sort of annual reports and then also transaction reports. And each of those things has its own range. And when you layer them on top of each other, the range just gets bigger and bigger and bigger.

DETROW: And I think that gets to something a lot of people are wondering - whether Trump or the people around him might have bought a lot of Nvidia stock over the weekend as it came together that Trump and a small circle knew that he was pressing Huang to be reinstated. When, if at all, would we get a picture of whether that sort of activity happened?

ALEXANDER: The most recent transaction reports that we received were just a few days ago, and they showed transactions from September. So you'd expect to see the batch that's referential to the time period that we're in right now in about two months. That being said, it's not all just about whether or not they were trading. They claim that third party people are managing his investment portfolio. Even if somebody else is trading it for you, if you hold a stock and you know that you own it, that can create a conflict of interest. Then the way to judge it is that if Trump had to follow the conflicts of interests laws that everybody else in the executive branch, other than the president and vice president, have to follow, what he's done over the last few days, making clear specific decisions related to a company that he owns in his personal portfolio, would be a federal crime.

DETROW: How does the way that the Trump White House approaches his trading of stocks, specifically Nvidia's stocks, track with the bigger picture of how Trump has approached his own personal finances during this presidency?

ALEXANDER: Well, Trump has been very involved in his personal holdings, setting aside the stock portfolio for a minute. I mean, the White House has claimed, for instance, that, you know, he's totally out of his business. I mean, I've done extensive reporting that just shows that that's not true at all. And the White House even confirmed to me that when he's at his golf club, he's making note of little details just as he does with the White House ballroom or something like that. So this is a guy who finds it difficult to be out of details that he's interested in. You know, he's not always in the details about everything, but when he wants to be in the details about something, he gets into the details about things.

DETROW: Yeah. So how does that frame how you think about decisions that he's made as he's been deeply personally involved in this Nvidia story, you know, knowing his relationship to Huang, knowing his holdings in this company. How are you thinking about the actions Trump has taken over the past few days?
